observables.label: noise x5 (U U-dagger U U-dagger U, 200 CZ)

answer:
I built the circuit for a line of 6 spins with H = sum of Z Z on neighbors plus sum of X (J = 1, h = 1). All spins start pointing up (bit 0), and the circuit evolves them to time 1. The circuit uses 4 second-order Trotter steps on Garnet qubits QB9, QB4, QB5, QB10, QB11, QB6. A perfect quantum computer running this circuit gives an average magnetization of +0.244. The exact continuous-time answer is +0.204. The gap of 0.04 comes from splitting time into 4 steps. It does not come from noise.

Next I made the stretched copies by gate folding. Folding replaces the circuit U with U, then U undone (U-dagger), then U again. In theory that does nothing, because the undo step cancels the extra U. On a real machine, every extra gate adds noise. So the x3 copy has 3 times the gates (120 two-qubit gates instead of 40), and the x5 copy has 5 times the gates (200). I folded the circuit after compiling it to Garnet's native gates, so the compiler could not cancel the extra gates. A noiseless check confirmed that all 3 copies still give +0.244.

I submitted all 3 circuits as one job with 4000 shots each to garnet:mock. The job ID is 01a16041-a4f9-70ba-966e-bcbba15a1560. The job finished with status DONE, and it cost no credits. The mock only checks that the job is valid. Its counts are random patterns (000000, 011011, 100100, 111111 in roughly equal shares), so they say nothing about physics. The counts_list field holds them as a record.

For realistic noisy numbers I ran the same 3 circuits on IQMFakeGarnet, the noisy Garnet simulator that comes with iqm-client. Each circuit got 4000 shots. The magnetization was +0.205 at noise x1, +0.153 at x3, and +0.123 at x5. Each one is below the ideal +0.244, and the value drops further as the noise grows.

To extrapolate, I fit a parabola through the 3 points (Richardson extrapolation) and read off its value at noise 0. That gives +0.239. The ideal value is +0.244. The raw x1 result was off by 0.039. The mitigated result is off by only 0.005. A straight-line fit gives +0.222, and an exponential fit gives +0.230. Both of these also land closer to the ideal than the raw value does. These numbers come from a single run, so shot noise of about 0.01 applies to each point.

This shows the principle behind IBM's 2023 utility experiment. You cannot remove the noise. You can make it larger on purpose and in a controlled way, measure how the answer changes, and then extrapolate back to zero noise. ZNE only removes errors caused by noise. It does not fix the Trotter step error, so the mitigated value targets +0.244 and not the exact +0.204.
